terms.definition: Application Programming Interface — a defined contract that lets two pieces of software talk to each other.
Software Development Kit — a bundle of tools, libraries and docs for building on a platform.
Command-Line Interface — a text-based way to run a program by typing commands.
Graphical User Interface — the windows, buttons and icons you click instead of typing commands.
Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery — automatically building, testing and shipping code on every change.
Minimum Viable Product — the smallest version of a product that delivers value and can be tested with real users.
Object-Relational Mapping — a library that lets you work with a database using objects instead of raw SQL.
Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic operations on stored data.
Representational State Transfer — a common style for web APIs built on standard HTTP verbs and URLs.
A high-performance remote-procedure-call framework from Google that uses HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers.
A query language for APIs that lets clients ask for exactly the data they need in one request.
JavaScript Object Notation — a lightweight, human-readable format for structured data.
YAML Ain't Markup Language — a human-friendly format often used for configuration files.
Structured Query Language — the standard language for querying relational databases.
A family of databases (document, key-value, graph) that don't use the traditional relational table model.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — guarantees that keep database transactions reliable.
Domain Name System — the internet's phone book, translating names like example.com into IP addresses.
Time To Live — how long a piece of data (a cache entry, DNS record, packet) stays valid before it expires.
Transport Layer Security — the encryption that secures web traffic (the 's' in HTTPS).
Virtual Private Network — an encrypted tunnel that routes your traffic through another network.
Content Delivery Network — a set of edge servers that cache content close to users for speed.
Service Level Agreement — a formal promise about uptime or performance, often with penalties.
Service Level Objective — the internal target for reliability that an SLA is built on.
Service Level Indicator — the actual measured value (e.g. error rate or latency) that an SLO is judged against.
JSON Web Token — a compact, signed token used to prove identity between services.
An open standard that lets an app access your data on another service without seeing your password.
Single Sign-On — logging in once to gain access to many separate applications.
Role-Based Access Control — granting permissions based on a user's role rather than per-person.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — browser rules controlling which sites may call a given API.
Cross-Site Scripting — a vulnerability where attackers inject malicious scripts into a web page.
Cross-Site Request Forgery — tricking a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted request.
Two-Factor Authentication — logging in with a password plus a second proof such as a phone code.
Large Language Model — an AI model trained on huge text corpora to understand and generate language.
Machine Learning — software that learns patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed.
Graphics Processing Unit — a highly parallel chip used for graphics and for training AI models.
Integrated Development Environment — an editor bundled with tools like a debugger and build runner.
Garbage Collection — automatic reclaiming of memory that a program no longer uses.
Out Of Memory — the condition where a process is killed for exhausting available RAM.
Kubernetes — a system for automating deployment, scaling and management of containers.
Infrastructure as Code — defining servers and networks in version-controlled config files.
Site Reliability Engineering — applying software-engineering practices to operations and uptime.
A culture and tooling that merges software development and IT operations for faster, safer releases.
Pull Request — a proposed set of code changes submitted for review before merging.
Work In Progress — something started but not finished; often a label on draft work.
Looks Good To Me — reviewer shorthand approving a change.
You Aren't Gonna Need It — advice not to build features before they're actually required.
Don't Repeat Yourself — a principle to avoid duplicating logic across a codebase.
Keep It Simple, Stupid — a reminder to prefer the simplest design that works.
Five object-oriented design principles (Single-responsibility, Open-closed, Liskov, Interface-segregation, Dependency-inversion) for maintainable code.
Regular Expression — a pattern language for searching and matching text.
An operation that has the same effect whether you run it once or many times.
A bug where the outcome depends on the unpredictable timing of concurrent operations.
A standstill where two tasks each wait forever for a resource the other holds.
The future cost of choosing a quick solution now over a better one that takes longer.
A switch that turns functionality on or off at runtime without redeploying code.
Releasing a change to a small subset of users first to catch problems before a full rollout.
A deploy strategy running two identical environments and switching traffic between them.
Reverting a system to a previous known-good version after a bad deploy.
An urgent patch applied directly to production to fix a critical issue.
A single repository that holds the code for many projects or services.
An application built, deployed and scaled as one large single unit.
An architecture that splits an app into small, independently deployable services.
A user-defined HTTP callback that a service sends when an event happens.
A cap on how many requests a client may make in a time window.
A guarantee that, given no new updates, all replicas of data will converge over time.
Wasting time arguing over trivial details while ignoring the important decisions.
Doing a long chain of seemingly unrelated tasks before you can do the thing you set out to do.
Debugging by explaining your code line-by-line to an inanimate object (or anyone) until the bug reveals itself.
Big-O notation — a way to describe how an algorithm's cost grows as input size grows.
Caching the result of an expensive function call so repeat calls return instantly.
A mechanism that slows producers when consumers can't keep up, preventing overload.
Test-Driven Development — write a failing test first, then the code that makes it pass.
Behavior-Driven Development — describe expected behavior in plain-language scenarios before coding.
An iterative approach to software delivery that ships small increments with frequent feedback.
An agile framework that organizes work into fixed-length sprints with defined roles and ceremonies.
A short, fixed time-box (often two weeks) in which a team commits to and completes a set of work.
A brief daily team sync where each person shares progress, plans and blockers.
Retrospective — a meeting to reflect on how the last sprint went and what to improve.
A workflow method that visualizes tasks on a board and limits work in progress.
The prioritized list of features and work a team has yet to pick up.
A relative estimate of how much effort a piece of work will take, used in agile planning.
Restructuring existing code to improve it without changing its external behavior.
A surface sign in code that hints at a deeper design problem.
A reusable, named solution to a commonly recurring software design problem.
A design pattern ensuring a class has only one shared instance across the program.
Supplying an object's dependencies from outside rather than creating them inside it.
Letting a single interface work with many different underlying types.
Bundling data with the methods that operate on it and hiding internal state.
Exposing only the essential details while hiding complexity behind a simpler interface.
A technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller inputs.
How an algorithm's running time grows as the input size grows.
How an algorithm's memory use grows as the input size grows.
A data structure mapping keys to values for near-constant-time lookup.
An O(log n) algorithm that finds an item by repeatedly halving a sorted range.
A linear data structure of nodes where each node points to the next.
Solving a problem by combining cached solutions to overlapping subproblems.
Last In, First Out — the ordering a stack uses: the most recent item comes out first.
First In, First Out — the ordering a queue uses: the oldest item comes out first.
Structuring a program so multiple tasks make progress in overlapping time periods.
Actually executing multiple computations at the same instant across multiple cores.
Mutual-Exclusion lock — ensures only one thread enters a critical section at a time.
A counter that limits how many threads may access a resource at once.
Asynchronous — work that runs without blocking the caller, delivering its result later.
A function passed into other code to be invoked later when an event or result occurs.
A function that captures and remembers variables from the scope where it was defined.
Data that cannot be changed after it is created.
A function whose output depends only on its inputs and which causes no side effects.
Any change a function makes beyond its return value, such as I/O or mutating state.
A component that spreads incoming traffic across multiple servers.
Splitting a database horizontally across machines so each holds only part of the data.
Keeping copies of data on multiple nodes for durability and read scaling.
In a distributed store you can guarantee at most two of Consistency, Availability and Partition-tolerance.
The time it takes for a single request to receive its response.
How many requests or operations a system can handle per unit of time.
Handling more load by adding more machines.
Handling more load by making a single machine more powerful.
A buffer that lets services hand off work to each other asynchronously.
Publish/Subscribe — a pattern where publishers broadcast events to many decoupled subscribers.
A safeguard that stops calling a failing dependency for a while so it can recover.
A single entry point that routes, authenticates and rate-limits calls to backend services.
Running code in managed, auto-scaling functions without provisioning or managing servers.
A client-supplied token that lets a server safely ignore duplicate requests.
The hard problem of detecting when cached data is stale and removing it.
Packaging an app with its dependencies into a portable, isolated container.
A popular platform for building, shipping and running application containers.
How well you can understand a system's internal state from its logs, metrics and traces.
99th-percentile latency — the value 99% of requests come in under; a measure of tail performance.
The smallest unit of execution the operating system schedules within a process.
When version control can't automatically reconcile competing edits to the same lines.
A test that passes and fails intermittently without any code change.
A tool that flags likely bugs and style problems in source code.
A pre-production environment that mirrors production for final testing before release.
A protocol giving a persistent, two-way connection between client and server.
Deliberately slowing or capping a client's request rate to protect a service.
HyperText Markup Language — the standard language for structuring web pages.
Cascading Style Sheets — the language that controls how web pages look.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — how browsers request web pages from servers.
HTTP Secure — HTTP encrypted with TLS so the connection stays private.
File Transfer Protocol — a standard way to upload and download files between computers.
Secure Shell — an encrypted protocol for logging into and running commands on remote machines.
Secure Sockets Layer — the older encryption for web traffic, now succeeded by TLS.
Transmission Control Protocol — a reliable, ordered way to send data across networks.
The core suite of protocols that the internet runs on.
Internet Protocol address — the numeric label identifying a device on a network.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol — automatically assigns IP addresses to devices.
Network Address Translation — lets many devices share one public IP address.
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol — a standard for querying directories like user accounts.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol — the standard protocol for sending email.
Internet Message Access Protocol — for reading email kept on a server.
Internet Service Provider — the company that supplies your internet connection.
Uniform Resource Locator — the address of a web page or resource.
Voice over IP — making phone calls over the internet instead of phone lines.
Wide Area Network — a network spanning a large area, like the internet.
Local Area Network — a network connecting devices in one location, like an office.
A server that sits between clients and the internet, forwarding and filtering requests.
A security system that monitors and controls network traffic by rules.
A small unit of data sent across a network.
An agreed set of rules for how computers exchange data.
High-speed, always-on internet access.
Delivering computing resources on demand over the internet.
eXtensible Markup Language — a flexible text format for structured data.
A technique for updating parts of a web page without a full reload.
The programming language that runs in web browsers to make pages interactive.
A popular server-side scripting language for building web pages.
A runtime that lets JavaScript run on servers, outside the browser.
A widely used open-source web server.
Software or a machine that serves web pages to browsers over HTTP.
A function exposed over a network so other software can call it.
Border Gateway Protocol — routes traffic between the large networks of the internet.
Peer-to-Peer — a network where computers share directly with no central server.
Really Simple Syndication — a format for subscribing to a site's updates.
Software whose source code is public to view, modify and share.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for a known security flaw.
Managed Service Provider — a company that remotely manages a client's IT.
Virtual LAN — a logically separated network running over shared physical hardware.
A modern image format with smaller file sizes than JPEG or PNG.
How many times per second a display updates its image, in hertz.
An old, unencrypted protocol for remote command-line access, superseded by SSH.
The algorithm that trains a neural network by propagating prediction errors backward through its layers to adjust the weights.
An optimization method that iteratively nudges a model's parameters in the direction that most reduces its error.
When a model learns the training data too closely — including its noise — and so performs poorly on new, unseen data.
The neural-network architecture behind modern language models; it uses attention to weigh how much each input token relates to the others.
A representation of text, images, or other data as a vector of numbers, so that similar items sit close together in that space.
A database that stores embeddings and finds the most similar ones quickly — the backbone of semantic search and RAG.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — feeding a language model relevant documents fetched at query time so its answers are grounded in real data.
Further training a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialize it.
Shrinking a model by storing its weights at lower numerical precision, trading a little accuracy for much less memory and faster inference.
The craft of wording instructions to a language model to get better, more reliable outputs.
When an AI model states something false or made-up as if it were fact.
Running a trained model on new input to get a prediction or output, as opposed to training it.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a language model can consider at once.
A generative model that creates images by starting from random noise and progressively denoising it.
Training an agent to make decisions by rewarding good actions and penalizing bad ones over many trials.
Training a model on labeled examples so it learns to predict the label for new inputs.
Finding structure or patterns in data that has no labels, such as clustering similar items.
A model loosely inspired by the brain, made of layers of interconnected nodes whose weights are learned from data.
Convolutional Neural Network — a neural network specialized for images that scans for visual patterns with sliding filters.
One complete pass of a training algorithm over the entire training dataset.
A configuration value set before training, like learning rate or batch size, that controls how a model learns.
Crafting and selecting the input variables that make a machine-learning model more accurate.
Machine Learning Operations — the practices and tooling for deploying, monitoring, and maintaining ML models in production.
The gradual decay of a model's accuracy as real-world data shifts away from what it was trained on.
Storing every change to application state as a sequence of events, so the current state can be rebuilt by replaying them.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation — separating the code that reads data from the code that writes it, so each can be optimized independently.
Managing a transaction that spans multiple services by chaining local steps, each with a compensating action to undo it on failure.
Releasing software by running two identical environments and switching traffic to the new one, allowing instant rollback.
Following a single request as it hops across many services, to pinpoint where time is spent or where it fails.
An infrastructure layer that handles service-to-service networking — routing, retries, security — without changing app code.
A helper container deployed alongside a main app to add capabilities like logging, proxying, or security.
The delay when a serverless function or app has to spin up from scratch before it can handle a request.
Managing infrastructure and deployments through Git, so the repository is the single source of truth for what's running.
Deliberately injecting failures into a system to test how resilient it is before real outages happen.
A shorthand for how an algorithm's time or memory grows as its input gets larger, such as O(n) or O(log n).
Automatic memory management that reclaims memory a program no longer uses.
A bug where a program keeps grabbing memory it never releases, slowly degrading or crashing it.
A bug or exploit where data written past the end of a buffer corrupts adjacent memory — a classic security hole.
An attack that sneaks malicious database commands into an app's input fields to read or destroy data.
A security model that trusts no user or device by default and verifies every request, even inside the network.
Multi-Factor Authentication — requiring two or more proofs of identity, like a password plus a phone code, to log in.
Scrambling data so only the sender and recipient can read it — not even the service carrying it.
Adding random data to a password before hashing it, so identical passwords don't produce identical hashes.
Encryption using a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt, so secrets can be shared without exchanging passwords.
Running computation close to where data is generated — near users or devices — instead of in a distant data center, to cut latency.
A server that sits in front of backend services, forwarding client requests and often handling caching, TLS, and load balancing.
At right angles in math — tech-speak for two things that are completely independent, so changing one doesn't affect the other.
A peak that's only the highest point nearby, not overall — used for a good-but-not-best situation you can't improve without first getting worse.
When a model is too simple to capture the real pattern in data — the opposite of overfitting.
A CPU swapping between tasks — used for the mental cost of jumping between unrelated pieces of work.
When requested data isn't in the fast cache and must be fetched slowly — used for failing to recall something you should know offhand.
Producing exactly the same output every time for the same input, with no randomness involved.
Involving randomness — a process whose outcomes follow probabilities rather than being exactly predictable.
A measure of disorder in physics and information theory — used for the natural tendency of systems, plans and codebases to drift into chaos.
How much useful information there is relative to meaningless noise — high signal means worth paying attention to.
Carrying a lot of useful information per unit of attention — tech-speak for dense, trustworthy input (people, meetings, or metrics).
When a system's output feeds back into its input, amplifying (positive loop) or damping (negative loop) the behavior over time.
The consequences of the consequences — the indirect downstream results of a decision that first-order thinking misses.
Reasoning up from basic fundamental truths instead of by analogy or convention — 'thinking from first principles'.
One component whose failure takes down the whole system — used for any person or process everything depends on.
Automatically switching to a backup system when the primary one fails.
Failing partially instead of completely — a system that keeps offering reduced service when parts of it break.
A bug that disappears or changes when you try to observe it — named after Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.
Rewriting a branch of work to sit on top of the latest changes in Git — used figuratively for re-grounding your view on new information.
A project built from scratch with no legacy constraints — the opposite of brownfield work inside an existing system.
An unusual situation at the boundary of what a system expects — where bugs, and exceptions to life plans, live.
The scenario where everything goes exactly as expected, with no errors or edge cases.
A quick basic test that a result isn't obviously wrong before trusting it.
A minimal first test that a system basically works at all — from powering on hardware and checking for smoke.
A practice execution that goes through all the steps without any real effect.
Using your own product day-to-day to find its problems — from 'eating your own dog food'.
Only ever moving in one direction — a value that always increases (or always decreases), never reversing.
A condition that must always hold true no matter what else changes — in code, and in tech-speak, in life plans.
The single authoritative, standard version of something — 'the canonical example'.
The minimum number of members that must agree for a decision to count, in distributed systems as in committees.
When two halves of a system lose contact and each carries on as if it were in charge — leading to conflicting versions of the truth.
When a huge number of waiting processes all wake and rush at once, overwhelming the very resource they waited for.
The difficulty of starting with no data, users or reputation — recommendation systems and new marketplaces both suffer it.
A reference that points at nothing, crashing the program when used — tech-speak for a reference to something that doesn't exist.
Segmentation fault — a crash from touching memory you don't own; used figuratively for a brain glitch mid-thought.
The lowest-level total crash an operating system can have — used figuratively for a complete mental shutdown.
When two different inputs produce the same hash fingerprint — two things that shouldn't be confusable colliding anyway.
A named container that keeps identifiers from clashing — why two functions (or two people named Alex) can coexist without confusion.
Physically isolating a system from all networks for security — used for keeping two parts of your life completely separate.
Every point where a system can be attacked — used figuratively for how exposed a plan or person is to criticism or failure.
A deliberate account of what you're defending against and from whom — 'what's your threat model?' asks which risks actually matter.
A group whose job is to attack your own system or plan to find weaknesses before real adversaries do.
A vulnerability unknown to the defender, exploitable with zero days of warning — a flaw nobody knew existed.
A decoy system left deliberately attractive to attackers so you can watch and catch them.
A single control that shuts the whole thing down instantly in an emergency.
A mechanism that triggers automatically if its operator stops checking in — protection that activates on silence.
A system that is always in exactly one of a defined set of states, with fixed rules for moving between them.
When the number of possible combinations grows so fast that checking them all becomes impossible.
Solving a problem by trying every possibility rather than by insight — guaranteed but expensive.
An approach that always grabs the best immediate option — fast, but it can lock you out of the best overall outcome.
A rule of thumb that's usually right and cheap to apply, traded against a guaranteed correct answer.
A system you can only judge by inputs and outputs because its inner workings are opaque.
The verified reality a model or belief is measured against — what actually happened, not what was predicted.
A test wrongly saying yes — flagging something that isn't actually there.
A test wrongly saying no — missing something that really is there.
A simplification that mostly hides complexity but fails in ways that force you to understand what's underneath.
A level of simplification that hides the messy details below so you can think at a higher level.
When two systems' fundamental shapes don't line up, so connecting them is permanently awkward — from electrical engineering.
A filter that lets slow signals through and blocks fast noise — used figuratively for ignoring hype and reacting only to trends.
The time for half of something to decay — used for how quickly knowledge, motivation or relevance fades.
Shrinking by a constant fraction each period — fast at first, then ever slower.
A factor of ten — 'an order of magnitude better' means roughly ten times, not just somewhat.
99.999% uptime — about five minutes of downtime a year; shorthand for extreme reliability.
The visual range of uncertainty around a measurement — 'big error bars' means the estimate could be far off.
The number of independent ways a system can vary — used for how much room to maneuver a person or plan really has.
The hidden internal map where an AI model organizes concepts by similarity — nearby points mean related ideas.
Having many independent variables at once — problems (and people) too complex to judge along a single axis.
The set of all possible answers to a problem — exploring it beats fixating on the first idea.
A constraint that forces action or a decision by making inaction impossible — deadlines are the classic one.
A sample size of one — an experiment or conclusion drawn from a single case, usually yourself.
How many observations a conclusion rests on — small samples make noisy, untrustworthy conclusions.
Torturing data with repeated analyses until something looks statistically significant — manufacturing a finding.
Unlikely to be explained by random chance alone — the conventional bar for a real effect in data.
What would have happened otherwise — the imagined alternative you compare against to judge a decision's real impact.
A hidden third factor that influences both things you're comparing, creating a false impression that one causes the other.
Recognizing a situation by its resemblance to past cases rather than analyzing it fresh — fast, but prone to stereotyping.
Structurally essential even if it doesn't look it — a 'load-bearing assumption' quietly holds the whole argument up.
One of the specific ways a system, plan or person characteristically breaks down.
Deliberately pushing a system past normal conditions to find where it breaks.
A (half-mythical) engineer ten times more productive than average — shorthand for outlier individual impact.
Change that happens in sudden jumps rather than gradually — 'a step-function improvement' is a discontinuous leap.
A sudden qualitative change when a threshold is crossed, like water to ice — small input, transformed system.
The initial energy needed to start a reaction — used for the hump of effort required to begin anything.
The observation that computing power per dollar doubles roughly every two years — shorthand for relentless exponential improvement.
Systems end up mirroring the communication structure of the organizations that build them.
Revising how strongly you believe something in proportion to new evidence — the rationalist ideal of changing your mind.
Rationalist-speak for revising your default assumptions after new evidence — from Bayesian probability.
Relating to knowledge and how confident you're entitled to be — 'epistemic humility' is knowing what you don't know.
Being pressured into action by a tiny probability of an astronomically huge payoff or catastrophe — exploiting expected-value reasoning.
Rationalist shorthand for the dynamics that make everyone race to the bottom even though no one wants to — coordination failure personified.
When the average across many people equals the average for one person over time — most of life is non-ergodic: you can't average away ruin.
How spread out outcomes are around the average — 'high variance' means big swings in either direction.
Extreme results tend to be followed by more ordinary ones — the sophomore slump is usually just statistics.
How common something is in general, before considering the specific case — ignoring it is a classic reasoning error.
Imitating the surface rituals of something successful without understanding what actually made it work.
Choosing to minimize your worst-case loss — planning against the strongest counter-move, from game theory.
Internet slang for someone smart enough to learn the sophisticated take but not enough to see why the simple answer was right — the middle of the bell-curve meme.
Mock praise for reasoning so many levels 'deep' it circles into absurdity — from the expanding-brain meme.
To understand something so completely it becomes intuitive — from Heinlein's 'Stranger in a Strange Land'.
A word or usage that instantly marks you as an insider or outsider of a group — vocabulary as a membership test.
Spreading and evolving like a virus of the mind — ideas selected for catchiness rather than truth.
An idea or group identity that takes on a life of its own and starts steering the people who created it — occult term adopted by internet rationalists.
Directly stimulating your own reward signal instead of doing the things the reward was for — the AI-safety metaphor for empty pleasure loops.
The formal description of what an agent is trying to maximize — tech-speak for someone's true priorities.
The things you want for their own sake, as opposed to instrumental values you only want as means to an end.
The AI-safety observation that almost any goal implies the same subgoals — acquire resources, survive, resist being switched off.
Someone's personal probability that AI causes human extinction or catastrophe — asked as 'what's your p(doom)?'.
Existential risk — a threat that could permanently destroy humanity's future, AI and pandemics being the usual examples.
Someone convinced things end badly — in AI circles, a person with a high p(doom).
Effective accelerationism — the pro-speed camp that wants technology (especially AI) built faster, opposing safety-first 'decels'.
Artificial General Intelligence — AI matching or exceeding humans across essentially all cognitive work.
The scenario where AI self-improves explosively in days or weeks rather than gradually — versus a slow, manageable soft takeoff.
The empirical finding that AI capability improves predictably as you add compute, data and model size.
The thought experiment of an AI that turns the universe into paperclips because that's literally what it was told to optimize — misalignment made vivid.
Acting autonomously toward goals rather than waiting for instructions — said of AI systems and, admiringly, of people.
About the actual substance of the matter, as opposed to meta-level discussion about how the discussion is going.
One step up from the substance — discussing the process, framing or pattern instead of the thing itself.
Gaming-speak for optimizing a build to maximize one stat and dump everything else — applied to lopsided life strategies.
Completing a game as fast as possible by exploiting every trick — used for blitzing through any process at record pace.
Gaming-speak for an optional detour from the main goal — a tangent adventure that isn't the mission.
Non-Player Character — gaming term repurposed as an insult for someone who seems to run on autopilot with no independent thoughts.
Gaming-speak for weakening something via an update — 'they nerfed it' means it got deliberately made worse.
The game about the game — the evolving layer of strategy about what everyone else is currently doing, where 'the meta' lives.
Random Number Generator — gaming shorthand for pure luck: 'that outcome was just RNG'.
Prompting an AI to reason step-by-step before answering — also tech-speak for showing your intermediate reasoning.
Teaching an AI a task from just a handful of examples in the prompt — versus zero-shot, with no examples at all.
Raw processing power as a resource — 'we don't have the compute' treats calculation capacity like fuel.
The dismissive description of large language models as mere remixers of training text with no real understanding.
Low-quality mass-produced AI-generated content flooding the internet — the spam of the generative era.
Bypassing a device's or AI's built-in restrictions to make it do things its maker forbade.
